growth_problem.classification_rule: no dominant pattern: none of the slowdown, collapse, volatility or growing rules fired
growth_problem.statement: The growth problem in French Polynesia is mixed, with no dominant pattern: growth of 1.0 percent a year over the last decade is neither a slowdown against the 20-year record, nor a recent collapse, nor unusually volatile, nor fast by the rubric's rules. GDP per capita growth over 2016–2025 (observed 2016–2024) averaged 1.0 percent a year (2006–2025 (observed 2006–2024): -0.1; no structural-peer median), with no convergence residual available and ranked 1 of 1 among structural peers. GDP per capita peaked in 1986, 38 years ago, and is 25.1 percent below that peak; a peak older than 30 years is context here, not the growth problem. A simplified single-break test finds a deceleration in 1975: average growth 2.3 percent before and -0.4 after. Investment (gross fixed capital formation to GDP) relative to expectation given income cannot be computed at 22.4 percent of GDP; the private-public split is unavailable in prototype (IMF Investment and Capital Stock Dataset not ingested). Gross savings relative to expectation given income cannot be computed; the current account balance is 5.8 percent of GDP and net FDI inflows are -0.2 percent of GDP. Structural change (G9) is not computed in the prototype. Exports to GDP relative to expectation given income cannot be computed. The relevant question is therefore: what holds back faster growth when neither the growth record nor investment shows a dominant pattern. Provisional top-split reading: indeterminate (no statistic available; not available: the real lending rate, real private credit growth, the investment residual).
